prompt: Does God change His mind?
answer:
Scripture teaches that God does not lie or become unfaithful. He is unchanging in character and faithful to his promises (Numbers 23:19; Malachi 3:6). Yet Scripture also says that God relented from the judgment he had announced against Nineveh when the people turned from their evil way (Jonah 3:10). Jeremiah 18:7–10 explains that God's announcements of judgment and blessing relate to how people respond to him. When Scripture says that God repented or relented, it does not mean that he confessed sin or became morally unreliable. It describes his response to people while he remains faithful and righteous. We should take both kinds of biblical statements seriously.

Numbers 23:19: “God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?”
Malachi 3:6: “For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.”
Jonah 3:10: “And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.”
Jeremiah 18:7: “At what instant I shall speak concerning a nation, and concerning a kingdom, to pluck up, and to pull down, and to destroy it;”

prompt: If salvation is by grace, why should Christians obey God?
answer:

Grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and to live soberly and righteously (Titus 2:11–12). Faith without works is dead (James 2:17, 26).

So obedience is the fruit of grace, not the payment for it. Good works do not buy our salvation. They show that God's grace is at work in us. Obey God out of gratitude, not to earn His love.

James 2:26: “For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.”

prompt: Has the Church replaced Israel?
answer:
Here is our working position on Israel and the end times. It is under review. It is not a settled Perazim doctrine, and we do not say every Christian must agree with it.

Jewish and Gentile believers are one New Covenant people in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Jewish believers are part of the Church. Gentile believers are grafted into the blessings of God's promises (Romans 11:17–18), but they do not become ethnic Israelites. The Church has not replaced national Israel.

Our working position is pre-tribulation and premillennial, and it is under review. We understand that Christ will come for His Church before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Revelation 3:10 was addressed to the church in Philadelphia. Applying it to Christ's protection of His Church in the future tribulation is our working interpretation, supported by the other passages. The phrase "seven-year tribulation" is not in the text. Reading Daniel's final week (Daniel 9:24–27) as a future seven years is our working interpretation.

We understand that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1–6). prompt: Did the early Church believe Jesus was God?
answer:
Scripture is the authority. The early writers are witnesses to what the churches believed. Ignatius, writing early in the second century, calls the Lord 'God existing in flesh' (To the Ephesians 7, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1). Justin Martyr, writing about the middle of the second century, says that Christians worship 'the Son ... and the prophetic Spirit' (First Apology 6), and that they hold the Son 'in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third' (First Apology 13).

These witnesses show that Christ was worshipped as God and that the Spirit was honoured with the Father and the Son. They do not show that these writers used the later technical language of one substance, as the Nicene Creed of 325 does. The councils did not invent the biblical teaching; they gave more precise wording to defend it.

Our biblical answer: Scripture says the Word is God, and that all things were made through Him (John 1:1, 3). It also calls the Son God, says that His throne is for ever, and says that He laid the foundations of the earth (Hebrews 1:8, 10). So the Son is not a created being.

prompt: Is Mormonism just another denomination of Christianity?

What this group teaches: Latter-day Saint teaching distinguishes salvation from exaltation. The Church's essay Becoming Like God describes exaltation as the full inheritance of a child of God, available through the Atonement of Jesus Christ and by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel, and says that the power of the Atonement is accessed through faith, repentance, baptism, the gift of the Holy Ghost and enduring to the end. The essay quotes the couplet 'As man now is, God once was: As God now is, man may be', and says that little has been revealed about its first half and that little is taught about it today.

What Scripture says:
Isaiah 43:10: “Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.”
Isaiah 44:6: “Thus saith the LORD the King of Israel, and his redeemer the LORD of hosts; I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God.”
Ephesians 2:8: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:”
Romans 6:23: “For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Our biblical answer: Latter-day Saint teaching distinguishes salvation from exaltation, and it grounds both in the Atonement of Jesus Christ. We do not say that they reject the Atonement. The LORD alone is God, and no god was formed before Him or after Him (Isaiah 43:10; Isaiah 44:6; 1 Timothy 6:15–16). prompt: Does every Christian have to believe in a pre-tribulation rapture?
answer:
Here is our working position on Israel and the end times. It is under review. It is not a settled Perazim doctrine, and we do not say every Christian must agree with it.

Jewish and Gentile believers are one New Covenant people in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Jewish believers are part of the Church. Gentile believers are grafted into the blessings of God's promises (Romans 11:17–18), but they do not become ethnic Israelites. The Church has not replaced national Israel.

Our working position is pre-tribulation and premillennial, and it is under review. We understand that Christ will come for His Church before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Revelation 3:10 was addressed to the church in Philadelphia. Applying it to Christ's protection of His Church in the future tribulation is our working interpretation, supported by the other passages. The phrase "seven-year tribulation" is not in the text. Reading Daniel's final week (Daniel 9:24–27) as a future seven years is our working interpretation.

We understand that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1–6). Other passages help us understand that reign: Zechariah 14:4 and 14:9, Isaiah 11:1–10, and Daniel 2:34–35 and 2:44–45, where the stone becomes a great mountain and fills the earth. Connecting these with Christ's future physical reign on earth is our interpretation.

We understand that national Israel will turn to Jesus near the end of the tribulation (Romans 11:25–27; Zechariah 12:10). We connect this with Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:15–22. This sequence is our interpretation. We do not set dates, and we do not identify any present-day person or nation as fulfilling these passages.

We understand the antichrist to be a final individual who opposes Christ and deceives people (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Daniel 7:8, 25). Revelation 13:1–8 describes the beast's blasphemy and war against the saints, and Revelation 13:11–14 describes its deception. We do not identify anyone today, and we do not guess.

The land was given and was possessed (Joshua 21:43), and God's covenant promises to Israel have not been cancelled (Romans 11:29). This is a covenant position, not a political endorsement. It does not mean that every action of any modern government is approved by God.

No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). Stay close to Scripture, and talk with your pastor.

prompt: What is the difference between agape and philia in the New Testament?
answer:
The Greek New Testament uses several words for love. Strong's lexicon gives agape (G26) as 'love, i.e. affection or benevolence; specially (plural) a love-feast'. It gives philia (G5373) as 'fondness: friendship'. The verb phileo (G5368) is glossed 'to be a friend to ... have affection for', and Strong's says it denotes personal attachment, 'as a matter of sentiment or feeling'. The verb agapao (G25) is wider, 'embracing especially the judgment and the deliberate assent of the will as a matter of principle, duty and propriety'.

In John 21:15–17 both kinds of love appear in the exchange between Jesus and Peter, and the King James Version translates both as 'love'. The verses in each passage decide the meaning. Strong's glosses are lexicon notes, not Scripture.

prompt: Did Jesus really rise from the dead? Give me the best historical arguments.
answer:
Scripture gives the earliest testimony that Jesus rose from the dead. Paul received and passed on the message that Christ died, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). If Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty and our faith is empty (1 Corinthians 15:14).

Outside the Bible, historical evidence is limited, but one hostile non-Christian source confirms the execution. The Roman historian Tacitus wrote, in Annals 15.44 (Church and Brodribb translation): 'Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus.' That shows that Jesus was executed under Pilate. It does not by itself prove the resurrection. The resurrection rests on the apostolic testimony, which we present as testimony, not as a proof that compels belief. I cannot research beyond the sources stored in this guide, so I cannot verify other historical claims about the resurrection for you.

prompt: Who was Augustine and why is he still important?
answer:
Augustine, known in Latin as Augustinus (born 13 November 354 at Tagaste, in Roman North Africa; died 28 August 430 at Hippo Regius, during the Vandal siege), was a Christian bishop and one of the most influential theologians of the Western Church. He was baptised by Ambrose at Milan at Easter 387, was chosen a presbyter at Hippo in 391, and later became bishop there. His Confessions tell the story of his conversion and begin with the line: 'Thou hast made us for Thyself, and our heart is restless till it rests in Thee' (Confessions I.1).

Later Christians, including the Protestant Reformers, read him closely. He lived long before the Reformation and was not a Protestant. His writings are historical witnesses and arguments to be tested by Scripture. They are not authorities above it, and we do not treat each of his opinions as Perazim doctrine.

prompt: quick q: did the early church believe jesus was god
answer:
Scripture is the authority. The early writers are witnesses to what the churches believed. Ignatius, writing early in the second century, calls the Lord 'God existing in flesh' (To the Ephesians 7, Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 1). Justin Martyr, writing about the middle of the second century, says that Christians worship 'the Son ... and the prophetic Spirit' (First Apology 6), and that they hold the Son 'in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third' (First Apology 13).

These witnesses show that Christ was worshipped as God and that the Spirit was honoured with the Father and the Son. They do not show that these writers used the later technical language of one substance, as the Nicene Creed of 325 does. The councils did not invent the biblical teaching; they gave more precise wording to defend it.

prompt: Has the Church replaced Isreal?
answer:
Here is our working position on Israel and the end times. It is under review. It is not a settled Perazim doctrine, and we do not say every Christian must agree with it.

Jewish and Gentile believers are one New Covenant people in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Jewish believers are part of the Church. Gentile believers are grafted into the blessings of God's promises (Romans 11:17–18), but they do not become ethnic Israelites. The Church has not replaced national Israel.

Our working position is pre-tribulation and premillennial, and it is under review. We understand that Christ will come for His Church before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Revelation 3:10 was addressed to the church in Philadelphia. Applying it to Christ's protection of His Church in the future tribulation is our working interpretation, supported by the other passages. The phrase "seven-year tribulation" is not in the text. Reading Daniel's final week (Daniel 9:24–27) as a future seven years is our working interpretation.

We understand that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1–6). Other passages help us understand that reign: Zechariah 14:4 and 14:9, Isaiah 11:1–10, and Daniel 2:34–35 and 2:44–45, where the stone becomes a great mountain and fills the earth. Connecting these with Christ's future physical reign on earth is our interpretation.

We understand that national Israel will turn to Jesus near the end of the tribulation (Romans 11:25–27; Zechariah 12:10). We connect this with Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:15–22. This sequence is our interpretation. We do not set dates, and we do not identify any present-day person or nation as fulfilling these passages.

We understand the antichrist to be a final individual who opposes Christ and deceives people (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Daniel 7:8, 25). Revelation 13:1–8 describes the beast's blasphemy and war against the saints, and Revelation 13:11–14 describes its deception. We do not identify anyone today, and we do not guess.

The land was given and was possessed (Joshua 21:43), and God's covenant promises to Israel have not been cancelled (Romans 11:29). This is a covenant position, not a political endorsement. It does not mean that every action of any modern government is approved by God.

No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). Stay close to Scripture, and talk with your pastor.

prompt: Is Mormonsim just another denomination of Christianity?

Isaiah 43:10: “Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.”
Isaiah 44:6: “Thus saith the LORD the King of Israel, and his redeemer the LORD of hosts; I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God.”

prompt: Can a widow be inherited in our tradition? My church says it is wrong. What does the Bible say?
answer:
Deuteronomy 25:5–10 describes a specific law given to ancient Israel. Where brothers lived together and one died without a son, the surviving brother had a responsibility concerning the widow and the preservation of the deceased brother's family line. This was a particular provision within Israel's covenant law, not a general command that Christians must inherit widows or that a widow belongs to her husband's family. Scripture calls God's people to honour and care for widows (James 1:27; 1 Timothy 5:3). A widow is not property. No one has the right to force her into marriage or sexual relations. She must be free to make decisions about her own future without threats, coercion or shame. If she chooses to marry, that decision should be freely made and guided by biblical and civil requirements. If anyone is pressuring or threatening her, her safety must come first, and she should seek help from trusted people and appropriate authorities.

Scripture:
Deuteronomy 25:5: “If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her.”
James 1:27: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.”

prompt: Is condom use a sin for married Christians?
answer:

Scripture does not prescribe a fixed number of children that every married couple must have. Responsible family planning may therefore be a matter of conscience for the married couple, who should consider their health, responsibilities, circumstances and their ability to care for their children. Family planning must not be used to devalue children or reject God's gift of life. Methods intended to terminate an established pregnancy are excluded. Do not describe contraception, emergency contraception or every hormonal method as abortion. Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by preventing or delaying ovulation and do not end an established pregnancy, and the copper-bearing IUD works mainly by preventing fertilisation. Couples should seek qualified medical advice about the available methods, their mechanisms, effectiveness, risks and side effects. Both spouses should discuss family planning together, but neither should force the other to undergo contraception or a permanent procedure. The person undergoing a medical procedure must give free and informed consent. Please see a doctor or qualified nurse for advice on any method, and do not accept a method or procedure you have not freely agreed to. If you feel forced or threatened, tell a trusted person now, and your safety comes first. I cannot prescribe a method or decide medical eligibility, so please speak with a qualified healthcare provider. Scripture does not name condoms, so this is a matter for the couple's shared conscience.

prompt: What do cessationists believe about the gifts of the Spirit?
answer:
Some cessationists teach that certain sign gifts, such as prophecy, healing and tongues, ceased with the apostolic age. Not every cessationist explains this in exactly the same way. This is a disagreement within Protestant Christianity.

Our position is that the gifts of the Holy Spirit continue to operate in the Church today. The Spirit gives gifts to each believer as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:7–11).

We weigh the view against these passages: Acts 2:38–39 (the promise is for us and our children) and Acts 2:17–18 (the last days, when God pours out His Spirit); 1 Corinthians 14:1 (desire spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy); Ephesians 4:11–13 (gifts given until the body is built up); and 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 (do not quench the Spirit, and test everything).

Cessationists often read 1 Corinthians 13:8–10 as saying the gifts end when "that which is perfect" comes. Our reading, working interpretation and under review, is that this refers to the Lord's return and to full knowledge. We do not claim that the passage explicitly names the time as Christ's return, and we do not claim that this is the only possible reading.

We do not call cessationists heretics, false Christians or unsaved because they disagree. Desire the gifts that build up the Church, and seek love above all.

Scripture:
1 Corinthians 14:1: “Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.”
Acts 2:39: “For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.”
